text_en: The Minotaur-C is a four-stage solid-fueled orbital launch vehicle developed by Orbital Sciences Corporation (now part of Northrop Grumman). Originally launched under the name *Taurus* in 1994, it was later rebranded as Minotaur-C to align with Orbital’s Minotaur family of rockets. The vehicle’s design integrates stages from the air-launched Pegasus rocket, combined with a first stage derived from the Peacekeeper intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM), repurposed for civilian space missions. This hybrid architecture allows Minotaur-C to deliver payloads of up to 1,458 kg (3,214 lb) into low Earth orbit (LEO), making it a cost-effective option for small satellite deployments. Its solid-fuel propulsion system, using PBHT propellant, simplifies operations by eliminating the need for complex liquid-fuel handling, though it lacks the ability to throttle or restart engines mid-flight. The launch site is SLC-576E at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, chosen for its polar orbit access, ideal for Earth observation satellites. Despite its reliability in many missions, Minotaur-C has faced setbacks, including three failures in ten launches, most notably the 2009 and 2011 mishaps that destroyed NASA’s OCO and Glory climate-monitoring satellites due to fairing separation issues—a flaw later corrected in subsequent iterations.
